bull.b: Sustained ~90% gross margins indicate robust per-unit economics that scale with volume. Strong product margins reduce the revenue required to reach profitability, allow pricing and promotional flexibility, and improve operating leverage over time if adoption continues.

bull.t: Early commercial traction and prescriber base
bull.b: Meaningful early prescription growth and a large prescriber footprint create a durable foundation for recurring sales. A broad and increasingly productive prescriber base reduces marginal marketing costs over time and supports scalable refill volumes as cohorts mature.

bull.t: Strong cash position and low leverage
bull.b: A large cash balance and negligible debt provide strategic runway to fund commercialization and operational improvements without immediate financing. Conservative leverage increases flexibility for investments, partnerships or to absorb execution setbacks during launch scaling.

bear.t: Large negative operating and free cash flow
bear.b: Persistent negative operating and free cash flow requires ongoing external capital unless revenue scales rapidly. Continued cash consumption constrains flexibility, heightens dilution risk, and forces prioritization of near-term commercial spend over long-term investments unless burn meaningfully declines.

Elevated SG&A relative to nascent revenue shows fixed-cost intensity from the launch. Unless revenue growth outpaces operating expense increases, reaching breakeven will require substantial and sustained volume gains, making profitability timing sensitive to commercialization execution.

bear.t: Uncertain refill dynamics and adoption pace
bear.b: Durable revenue depends on refill persistence and routine prescribing. Lack of granular cohort refill data and slower new-patient adoption create uncertainty in lifetime value, complicate forecasting, and may require sustained promotional spend to overcome physician behavior barriers.
